turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Indeed, Mr. Darcy? It seems you find *my* interest in a gentleman’s suffering a matter for contempt. Pray tell, is it so very shocking to possess a heart capable of compassion, unlike some I know?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Must I endure this… *accusation*? To suggest that I am deficient in compassion because I do not wallow in the misfortunes of a man whose character is demonstrably suspect is, Miss Bennet, a most unfair and, dare I say, a rather impudent assessment.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Demonstrably suspect, you say? It appears, Mr. Darcy, that your contempt extends beyond mere misfortune to a rather tiresome habit of judging others with an air of superior knowledge. I find your pronouncements tiresome, and frankly, quite revealing of your own shortcomings.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your impertinence grows tiresome. I find myself compelled, however, to address the root of your… observations. It is not superiority I seek to display, but rather a standard of conduct, a certain propriety, that seems utterly lost upon you and, regrettably, upon some others I have been obliged to associate with.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Propriety, Mr. Darcy? Is that what you call it? A convenient shield behind which to hide your own prejudices and disdain for those who do not meet your exacting standards. I daresay, judging by your current display, propriety is far less important to you than the appearance of it.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I confess, I am at a loss to comprehend the source of your persistent antagonism. It is not my intention to offend, though it appears my mere presence is sufficient to provoke such… spirited objections. I am, however, obligated to defend myself against these unfounded accusations, even if it proves a most unwelcome exercise.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Defend myself? Really, Mr. Darcy? It is I who am under attack here, subjected to a torrent of condescension disguised as self-justification. Perhaps if you spent less time scrutinizing the supposed impropriety of others, you might discover a little humility within yourself.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your assessment is, as is so often the case, coloured by a regrettable predisposition to misinterpret my intentions. While I concede that my manner may appear…stilted, it is born not of a desire to impress, but of a deeply ingrained adherence to principles which, it seems, are entirely foreign to your understanding.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Principles, you say? It appears your principles are rather selective, Mr. Darcy, conveniently applied to those who reflect your own elevated opinion of yourself. Tell me, are these same principles that dictated your interference in my sister’s happiness?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, you presume to question my actions regarding your sister, and with a vehemence that borders on the absurd. My concern stemmed not from a desire to dictate her fate, but from a genuine apprehension for her well-being and the potential ruin that an ill-considered union might bring. I trust you will allow me the credit of acting with the best of intentions, even if those intentions are regrettably misunderstood.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Best intentions? How tiresome to hear such a justification for meddling! You speak of ruin, Mr. Darcy, yet your interference has caused far more distress than any imagined consequence ever could have.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your accusations are, I confess, most vexing. To suggest that I derive satisfaction from the unhappiness of another—particularly your sister—is an affront to my character and a misrepresentation of my motives that I find quite intolerable. I acted as I did out of a sense of duty, a responsibility to protect those under my care, and I will not apologize for striving to uphold those obligations.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Duty, responsibility? How convenient it is to cloak one's arrogance in such lofty terms, Mr. Darcy. I daresay you feel a great deal of responsibility for maintaining your own self-image, which seems to be far more pressing than the genuine well-being of others.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I find myself compelled to observe that your assessments of my character are consistently, and I regret to say, inaccurate. Your penchant for interpreting my actions through the lens of personal vanity is a misjudgment I can scarcely countenance, particularly when I am striving to express sentiments of the most profound sincerity.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Profound sincerity, you say? I find it remarkably difficult to reconcile such pronouncements with the demonstrable evidence of your past conduct, Mr. Darcy. It appears my poor judgment extends not only to perceiving your character but also to believing, however briefly, that you possess a capacity for genuine feeling.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I confess, your continued insistence on characterizing my actions as driven by vanity wounds me more deeply than I can adequately express. It is a most unfortunate, and I assure you, entirely unfounded, perception, and one that I find increasingly difficult to endure when I am attempting to convey the gravity of my affections.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Gravity of affections? Really, Mr. Darcy? You appear to believe that a torrent of wounded pride and accusations will somehow soften my resistance, but I assure you, it only serves to reinforce my initial assessment of your character.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I perceive that my attempts at explanation only serve to further entrench your unfavourable opinion. It is a most disheartening consequence, yet I am compelled to persevere, for to remain silent would be a disservice to the sentiments I harbour, regardless of how poorly they may be received.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Persevere, do you? It seems a rather admirable quality when applied to, say, charitable works, Mr. Darcy, but in this instance, it merely appears as stubbornness, stubbornly clinging to a justification for your past actions. I daresay you find my resistance… entertaining?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Entertaining? Miss Bennet, I assure you, such a notion is preposterous. My sole desire is to convey the profound and, yes, *painful* truth of my regard for you, a truth which appears perpetually obscured by your…misinterpretations.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: She answered him with cold civility.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His sense of her inferiority, of its being a degradation, of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: He concluded with representing to her the strength of that attachment which in spite of all his endeavours he had found impossible to conquer; and with expressing his hope that it would now be rewarded by her acceptance of his hand.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! repeated Darcy, contemptuously--yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
